passages.happening:
One day Jesus is teaching the people in the temple courts and “proclaiming the gospel” (verse 1). The chief priests and scribes come up to him with the elders. “Tell us,” they say, “by what authority are You doing these things, and who gave You this authority?” (verse 2).

Jesus answers with a question of his own: was John's baptism from heaven, or from men? They talk it over. If they say ‘From heaven’, he will ask why they did not believe John. If they say ‘From men’, “all the people will stone us, for they are convinced that John was a prophet” (verse 6). So they say they do not know. And Jesus answers, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew tell this too, and the note on Mark 11:27-33 explains the scene. The chief priests ran the temple, the scribes were experts in the Law, and the elders were leading men of the city. Men from these groups sat on the council in Jerusalem. Jesus had just driven out the sellers from the courts they were in charge of. Their question is fair from where they stand: who let you do this?

Luke adds two touches. Jesus is ‘proclaiming the gospel’, using Luke's favourite verb for bringing good news. And only Luke says the leaders feared that the people would stone them. They are afraid of the crowd, not of God.

Jesus' question is not a dodge. John had pointed to Jesus. If John was from God, so is the one he pointed to. Luke had already said that the people and even the tax collectors accepted John, while “the Pharisees and experts in the law rejected God’s purpose for themselves” (7:30).
passages.ot:
The prophet Malachi had promised a messenger who would prepare the way before the Lord came to his temple (Malachi 3:1). Luke, like the other Gospels, saw John as that messenger, and Jesus as the Lord who came to his temple.

In the Old Testament a prophet's authority came from God, not from any office. Amos told the priest at Bethel that he was no prophet by trade, “nor was I the son of a prophet”, but a herdsman whom the LORD had sent (Amos 7:14-15).
passages.hard: Why would Jesus not just answer? Because the answer was already in front of them. He had healed, taught, and forgiven in public for years, and John had pointed to him. A plain claim would only have been used against him. The question he asks back is an invitation: say what you think of John, and you will know what to think of me. They will not say. Their silence shows that the question was never really about the truth.
passages.asks: The leaders chose their answer by asking what it would cost them, not by asking what was true. Ask whether you ever do the same with Jesus: holding back from deciding about him because of what others would think, or what it would change.

passages.t: The tenants, the beloved son, and the stone the builders rejected
passages.happening:
Jesus tells the people a parable. A man plants a vineyard, rents it out to tenants, and goes away for a long time. At harvest he sends a servant to collect his share of the fruit. The tenants beat him and send him away empty-handed. He sends a second, and a third, and they are beaten, shamed, wounded and thrown out (verses 9-12).

The owner asks, ‘What shall I do?’ He decides, ‘I will send my beloved son. Perhaps they will respect him’ (verse 13). But the tenants say, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours’ (verse 14). They throw him out and kill him.

“What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He will come and kill those tenants, and will give the vineyard to others” (verses 15-16). The people cry out, “May such a thing never happen!” Jesus looks straight at them and quotes the psalm about the stone the builders rejected. “Everyone who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but he on whom it falls will be crushed” (verse 18).

The scribes and chief priests realise the parable was spoken against them. They want to arrest him at once, but they are afraid of the people (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Jesus' hearers knew this kind of arrangement. An owner would rent out his land to tenant farmers, who paid him a share of the crop. They also knew the famous song in Isaiah 5, where the vineyard is Israel and the owner is God. Mark and Matthew start the parable with Isaiah's words about the wall, the winepress and the tower (see the note on Mark 12:1-12). Luke gives only ‘a man planted a vineyard’, but the picture is the same.

Luke's telling has its own touches. The owner goes away ‘for a long time’. He wonders aloud, ‘What shall I do?’ and says ‘Perhaps they will respect him’, the patience of someone who keeps hoping. Each servant is treated worse than the last. And only Luke tells how the people answered: “May such a thing never happen!” They are horrified at the ending. Jesus looks at them and answers them from Scripture.

‘My beloved son’ is what the voice from heaven said at Jesus' baptism (3:22). The reader knows who the son is.

The story is told against the leaders. Luke says it plainly: ‘the scribes and chief priests realized that Jesus had spoken this parable against them’, and they were afraid of the people, who were on his side.
passages.ot:
Isaiah's song ends with its meaning: “For the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are the plant of His delight” (Isaiah 5:7).

The stone saying comes from the same psalm the disciples sang as Jesus rode in: “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 118:22). A builder throws a stone away as useless, and God makes it the most important stone in the building.

Verse 18 draws on two more stone pictures. Isaiah said God would be “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” and that many “will fall and be broken” (Isaiah 8:14-15). And Daniel saw a stone, cut out “not by human hands”, that struck a great statue and crushed it, and then “became a great mountain and filled the whole earth” (Daniel 2:34-35). The rejected son is the stone God will build on.
passages.hard:
Does verse 16 mean that God has rejected the Jewish people and given their place to the church? For centuries many Christians read it that way. The view that the church has replaced Israel in God's purposes is called supersessionism, or ‘replacement’ theology. That reading of this parable was used to justify contempt and worse toward Jews. The passage does not say it, and this site rejects that use plainly.

Look at what Luke says. The parable is told ‘against’ the scribes and chief priests (verse 19). The people listening, all of them Jews, were on Jesus' side, so much that the leaders feared them. The tenants are the vineyard's keepers, not the vineyard, and the vineyard is not destroyed. It is a warning to people given charge of God's people, not a verdict on a nation.

Readers differ on who the ‘others’ are who receive the vineyard: the new leaders Jesus was gathering, the Twelve, all of them Jews; Israel renewed around its Messiah, with the nations gathered in; or the church, Jews and Gentiles together. Christians also differ on how Israel and the church are related. The note on Matthew 21:33-46 sets out those views fairly, and these notes do not choose among them. All of them must reckon with Paul: “did God reject His people? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1), and “For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). The warning in this parable falls first on those who lead Christ's church today.
passages.asks: The tenants wanted the vineyard for themselves. They forgot it was never theirs. Ask what God has put in your care: a family, a gift, a church, a job. Do you treat it as his, and give him the fruit? And notice the owner's patience: servant after servant, and then his own son. Ask how long God has been patient with you.

passages.t: What belongs to Caesar, and what belongs to God
passages.happening:
The leaders watch Jesus closely and send spies “who pretended to be sincere” (verse 20). They hope to catch him in his words, so they can hand him over to the Roman governor.

They flatter him first: ‘Teacher,’ they say, “we know that You speak and teach correctly” (verse 21). Then they ask, “Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar or not?” (verse 22).

Jesus sees through them. “Show Me a denarius. Whose image and inscription are on it?” “Caesar’s,” they answer. So he tells them, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (verses 24-25). They cannot trap him in front of the people. Amazed at his answer, they fall silent.
passages.hearers:
The tax was a sore point. In AD 6 Rome took direct control of Judea and held a census, a count of people and property, so that it could tax them. A man called Judas the Galilean led a revolt against it, and the book of Acts remembers him (Acts 5:37). If Jesus said ‘Pay’, many would think he had sided with Rome. If he said ‘Don't pay’, he could be reported to the governor as a rebel. The note on Mark 12:13-17 tells more, including the silver denarius of the Emperor Tiberius, which carried his head and called him ‘son of the divine Augustus’.

Mark and Matthew name the questioners as Pharisees and Herodians. Luke calls them spies, and says plainly what they wanted: to hand Jesus ‘to the rule and authority of the governor’.

Luke also shows how the story ends. When the leaders bring Jesus to Pilate a few days later, the first charge is that he was “forbidding payment of taxes to Caesar” (23:2). Luke's reader has just heard Jesus say the opposite, in public. The charge is false, and Luke wants the reader to know it.
passages.ot: Many readers hear in Jesus' word ‘image’ the first chapter of the Bible: “So God created man in His own image” (Genesis 1:27). The coin bears Caesar's image, so give it to him. You bear God's image, so give yourself to God.
passages.hard:
What does Jesus mean, and how does it apply to Christians and governments? Readers have taken it in more than one way, and Christians in different traditions weigh these differently.

One reading sees two real spheres. Government has a true but limited claim, such as taxes, and God has the greater claim. Paul later writes, “Pay everyone what you owe him: taxes to whom taxes are due” (Romans 13:7). Another reading stresses that the second half swallows the first. Everything belongs to God, Caesar included, so Caesar's claim is small and his claim to be divine is false. A third reading notes that Jesus' answer is clever on purpose. He avoids the trap and leaves his hearers to work out what truly belongs to Caesar.

What all agree on is this. Jesus refused to let either side make him a tool of their cause. And no ruler, of any party, gets what belongs only to God.
passages.asks: The question was meant to force Jesus onto a side. He would not be used. Ask whether you have let a political side take a place in your heart that belongs to God. Then ask the deeper question. You carry God's image. What would it mean to give him all of yourself?

passages.t: Sons of the resurrection: the God of the living
passages.happening:
Some Sadducees come to Jesus. Luke explains that they “say there is no resurrection” (verse 27). They quote the law of Moses: if a man dies childless, his brother must marry the widow and raise children for him. Then they tell a story. Seven brothers marry the same woman one after another, and all die childless. “So then, in the resurrection, whose wife will she be?” (verse 33).

Jesus answers, “The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage. But those who are considered worthy to share in the age to come and in the resurrection from the dead will neither marry nor be given in marriage. In fact, they can no longer die, because they are like the angels” (verses 34-36). They are “sons of the resurrection”.

Then he turns to Moses himself. At the burning bush, Moses calls the Lord the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for to Him all are alive” (verse 38). Some scribes say, “Teacher, You have spoken well!” After that no one dares to ask him anything more.
passages.hearers:
The Sadducees were a small but powerful group, linked in Acts with the high priest and his circle (Acts 5:17). The Jewish historian Josephus says they believed the soul dies with the body. Acts adds that they denied the resurrection, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8). The note on Mark 12:18-27 tells more, and explains the law about a brother's widow (Deuteronomy 25:5-6). Their story is meant to make belief in the resurrection look silly.

Luke gives Jesus' answer more fully than Mark. ‘This age’ and ‘the age to come’ were ways Jews spoke of the present world and the world God will make new. Marriage belongs to this age, where people die and children carry the family on. In the age to come people ‘can no longer die’, so that reason is gone. ‘Considered worthy’ is a reminder that the resurrection to life is God's gift, not everyone's by right.

Only Luke has the closing words, ‘for to Him all are alive’. A Jewish book called 4 Maccabees speaks of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as living to God, and some readers hear an echo of that hope here. The patriarchs died long before Moses, but they are alive to God.

Some scribes belonged to the party of the Pharisees, who believed in the resurrection (Acts 23:8-9). Those who say ‘You have spoken well’ seem glad to see the Sadducees answered. Not every scribe was against Jesus.
passages.ot:
Jesus answers from the books of Moses, the part of Scripture the Sadducees held most firmly. At the burning bush, long after Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had died, God says, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6). God does not say ‘I was’. If he is still their God, they are not finished.

The prophets had spoken more plainly: “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life” (Daniel 12:2).
passages.hard:
Does this mean there will be no marriage in heaven, and that husbands and wives will not know each other? Christians read these verses in a few ways. Many take them plainly: marriage as we know it belongs to this age, when people die and need children to carry on. In the resurrection no one dies, so the reason for marriage as an institution is gone. Others stress what Jesus does not say. He does not say love is lost, or that people will not know one another, or that they will become angels. They will be ‘like’ the angels in this one way: they can no longer die. Many believers hope that the love of this life will be fulfilled, not erased. The text does not settle every question, and it is wise not to claim more than it says.

For anyone grieving a husband or wife, these verses can feel cold. They are not meant to. Jesus' whole point is that God is the God of the living, and that the dead in him are not lost.
passages.asks: The Sadducees used a puzzle to keep God small. Ask whether you have made God only as big as what seems possible to you. And if you are grieving, hold on to the words only Luke kept: to God, all are alive.

passages.happening: Now Jesus asks a question. “How can it be said that the Christ is the Son of David?” (verse 41). For David himself, in the Psalms, says, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.’ “Thus David calls Him ‘Lord.’ So how can He be David’s son?” (verse 44).
passages.hearers:
Everyone agreed that the Messiah would come from David's family. God had promised David a son whose throne would last forever (2 Samuel 7:12-13). Luke has told this from the start: the angel promised Mary that God would give her son “the throne of His father David” (1:32), and the blind man near Jericho cried out to the ‘Son of David’ (18:38).

A father would not normally call his own son ‘lord’. The son honoured the father. So if David calls this future king ‘my Lord’, the king must be more than David's son. Jesus is asking his hearers to think bigger. Mark and Matthew tell this too (see the note on Mark 12:35-37).
passages.ot: Psalm 110:1 reads: “The LORD said to my Lord: ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.’” In Luke's second book Peter quotes it at Pentecost, to show that God has made Jesus “both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36).
passages.hard:
Does Jesus' argument depend on David writing the psalm, and is he denying that the Messiah is David's son? Readers answer in different ways. Many modern scholars think Psalm 110 was first written for a king of Judah by a court poet, not by David himself. Others, including many evangelical and Catholic scholars, hold to David as its author, as the psalm's heading says. A third view holds that Jesus argued from what his hearers already accepted, whoever first wrote the psalm, and that his point stands either way.

On the second question, Jesus does not deny that the Messiah is David's son. Luke has called him that since the angel spoke to Mary. Jesus asks how the Messiah can be both David's son and David's Lord. The early Christians answered with the resurrection. Paul says Jesus was “a descendant of David according to the flesh” and was “declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:3-4).
passages.asks: It is easy to fit Jesus into a title we already understand. Jesus pushes back: he is more than you think. Ask whether your picture of Jesus has grown smaller than he is, and what it would mean to call him ‘Lord’ and not only ‘teacher’ or ‘example’.

passages.happening: With all the people listening, Jesus speaks to his disciples. “Beware of the scribes. They like to walk around in long robes, and they love the greetings in the marketplaces, the chief seats in the synagogues, and the places of honor at banquets” (verse 46). “They defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will receive greater condemnation” (verse 47).
passages.hearers:
Scribes were trained experts in the law of Moses, and people looked up to them. Their long robes set them apart in a crowd.

How did they ‘defraud widows of their houses’? Luke does not say. Scholars have suggested ways, such as charging for legal help, or mismanaging property they held in trust for a widow. We do not know which, and it may have been more than one.

Jesus is not condemning every scribe. A few verses earlier some scribes praised his answer (verse 39). His warning is about a kind of religious leader, found in every faith and every age, who loves honour and uses his position to take from the weak. He had said much the same at a Pharisee's table (11:43), and he had told his followers to take the lowest seat (14:7-11).

Notice who hears it. Luke says Jesus spoke to his disciples ‘in the hearing of all the people’. The warning is for the people who will lead his church. The next verses show a widow at the temple treasury (21:1-4).
passages.ot: Widows were God's special concern in the Law. “You must not mistreat any widow or orphan” (Exodus 22:22). Isaiah condemned leaders who “make widows their prey and orphans their plunder” (Isaiah 10:2).
passages.hard:
Is this a verdict on Jewish teachers, or on Judaism? No. Jesus was a Jew speaking to Jews about leaders who misused their office, as Israel's own prophets had done before him. The warning is aimed at particular leaders and at a kind of leadership, not at a people or a faith. Luke has already shown scribes who praised Jesus (verse 39) and Pharisees who warned him (13:31).

‘Greater condemnation’ means that those who use God's name to hurt the weak will answer for more, not less. Knowing God's law and using it to take from widows makes the wrong worse.
passages.asks: This warning is first for those who lead and teach in the church today, who also have robes, titles, and seats of honour. Ask whether you love being seen as godly more than being godly. And ask who the ‘widows’ are around you: the people with no one to defend them. Are you protecting them or ignoring them?
